Photograph: Gavriil Grigorov/Reuters View image in fullscreen Vladimir Putin watches a missile launch from the Varyag during the Russian Pacific fleet exercises. Photograph: Gavriil Grigorov/Reuters Japan Russia’s missile tests around disputed islands anger Japan Pacific fleet launched missile drills near what Moscow calls the Kuril Islands but Japan regards as its Northern Territories Gavin Blair in Tokyo Fri 21 Aug 2026 00.54 EDT Last modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 01.03 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Japan has criticised missile tests carried out by Russia’s navy around the disputed islands visited by Vladimir Putin last week amid continuing tensions between the two countries. Russia’s Pacific fleet said on Thursday that it had fired Bastion surface-to-ship missiles from Etorofu, the largest island in the disputed archipelago, simulating an attack on enemy vessels, hitting all of its targets approximately 300km away. Officials said the drills included a nuclear-powered submarine and a guided-missile cruiser, according to reports. Putin sparked a tit-for-tat summoning of ambassadors in Tokyo and Moscow with his first visit last week to Etorofu, the largest of the group of four islands. They are referred to as the Northern Territories or Four Northern Islands in Japan , and as part of the Kuril Islands in Russia. Toshimitsu Motegi, Japan’s foreign minister, said on Thursday during a trip to Oman: “We cannot tolerate moves to strengthen military power on the Four Northern Islands because they go against our country’s stance [on the territories].” The Kuril Islands: how a visit from Putin reignited a 150-year-old dispute between Japan and Russia Read more Territorial rows over the islands go back to the 19th century. The Soviet Union seized them from Japan at the end of the second world war. Exercises by the Russian fleet began on 4 August and Japan was informed in advance that they would include live-fire drills. Japan lodged a protest against the large-scale manoeuvres on 5 August. According to the Russian news agency Tass, the drills involved “approximately 60 surface ships, submarines, and support vessels, about 30 aircraft, helicopters, and unmanned aerial systems of the Pacific fleet’s naval aviation, as well as over 13,000 service members”. Putin observed some of the exercises from the Varyag on 12 August as part of his trip to the disputed islands and to Sakhalin, the large undisputedly Russian island north of Hokkaido. “The region is unfortunately becoming increasingly prone to conflict, with Nato seeking to gain a foothold here and the emergence of new military and political blocs,” said Putin, speaking aboard the flagship. “There are efforts and plans to deploy new weapons systems here, which creates threats for our country.” The Russian drills are scheduled to continue through 29 August. https://www.cp24.com/news/canada/2026/08.text: RIGA — As Russian threats escalate in Latvia, a Canadian-led NATO mission is strengthening its presence near the Russian and Belarusian borders. The Canadian Press observed the increasing tensions on the ground. In the early hours of Aug. 14, residents in four areas of the region received a phone alert, including in Daugavpils, Latvia’s second-largest city. The alert urged citizens to take shelter due to a “potential threat” detected in the airspace. Jana, a Russian-speaking Latvian woman whom The Canadian Press met outside a church in Daugavpils, was among the tens of thousands of people who received the alert. “Obviously, it’s very worrying to receive this kind of message. We worry about our family, about our loved ones. Only crazy people aren’t worried,” said Jana, who did not want to give her full name to the media. A few hours after the alert, authorities announced that a drone loaded with explosives originating from Belarus had violated Latvian airspace before being shot down by NATO fighter jets. No injuries were reported. Tensions between Latvia, Moscow and Minsk have increased to the point where Latvian Prime Minister Evika Silina was forced to resign last May, following repeated incursions by unmanned aerial vehicles into the country’s territory. The Canadian Press met with Canadian Col. David Brassard, the newly appointed commander of the NATO Multinational Brigade in Latvia, at the Adazi military base, located in the centre of the country. He took office on June 10, two weeks after Silina’s resignation. Since then, he says three drones have been shot down. “The security situation we are currently experiencing in the east is what I call a ‘hybrid’ situation,” he said. “Hybrid” attacks refer to hostilities that do not necessarily constitute formal acts of war but aim to destabilize governments and sow confusion among the population. Those responsible for such acts are not always easily identifiable. “It’s not as if there were Russian flags attached to the drones; it can be difficult to assign blame,” said Brassard. Some of these drones are reportedly Ukrainian drones that were diverted into Latvian airspace by Russian jamming, he added. Maj.-Gen. Arnoud Stallmann of NATO’s Allied Command Transformation does not hesitate to use the word “war” to describe the situation. “We have truly come to terms with the threat from Russia; even though, at this stage, we call it hybrid war, I think we are actually at war,” Stallmann said during a NATO exercise in Selijas, central Latvia, in mid-August. The Canadian mission aims to “reassure, deter, and defend,” and is adapting to the escalation of hostile acts. Since the mission’s launch in 2017, Canadian troops — numbering between 1,500 and 1,600 — have been stationed in Adazi. But they will now be increasingly deployed, sometimes on a permanent basis, to various strategic locations near the borders with Russia and Belarus. “This is just the beginning. We’re in the process of expanding between now and Christmas,” said Brassard, noting that a first permanent platoon is now stationed in the Russian-speaking city of Daugavpils. “There are subversive activities taking place around Daugavpils, a culturally Russian region with strong ties to Russia,” Brassard said. In Latvia, Russian speakers account for about 30 per cent of the total population. In Daugavpils, the proportion is closer to 80 per cent. On the streets of Daugavpils, several residents interviewed by The Canadian Press are opposed to NATO’s military presence in their city. “We don’t need NATO. I see Canadian soldiers in the city, always eating kebabs. Why are they here? I don’t understand what purpose they serve,” said Mikhail, a 55-year-old man who served in the Soviet Army. Inna Plavoka, editor-in-chief of the independent media outlet Chayka, which publishes content primarily in Russian, is more sympathetic to NATO. “It may be hard for a Canadian to understand their position, but you have to realize that Russian propaganda is so effective at brainwashing people,” she said. When the war in Ukraine broke out, she says many believed “the Russians will take care of the Ukrainians and then come to save us.” When she asked who they wanted to be saved from, “they made the usual argument that the Russian language is being suppressed.” In Latvia, a country that endured 50 years of Soviet occupation, many Russian speakers feel discriminated against due to national policies that restrict the use of Russian in education and public spaces. Russian President Vladimir Putin often uses the pretext of defending Russian-speaking populations to justify his offensives in Ukraine. Latvian speakers generally hold a very positive view of the Canadian presence. A 2022 study by the University of Greifswald in Germany in collaboration with the Latvian research centre SKDS found that 79 per cent of them described Canadian soldiers as being professional or friendly. The same study shows that 34 per cent of Russian speakers find it difficult to characterize Canadian troops. Brassard says his troops are “prepared” for a Russian incursion into Latvia, adding he has “all the capabilities (he) needs” to deal with an attack. How likely is a Russian attack? “It’s a question of capabilities and intentions,” answers Janis Kazocins, who served as the Latvian president’s national security adviser from 2016 to 2023. He says the Kremlin would “certainly” intend to take economic, political and military control of the Baltic states if possible. “The real question is whether the Russians are willing to risk a nuclear war over a small town in northeastern Estonia or Latvia,” he argued. But Kazocins, who is now with the Riga Center for Geopolitical Studies, does not believe there’s a serious risk of a conventional attack against NATO. “Russia does not have the capacity to open a new front,” he says. “It simply wouldn’t work, especially since we have people — like your fellow Canadians — who actively support us on the ground and who, in the event of an attack, will fight.” Young people have also expressed their willingness to fight for their country. A drone believed to come from Belarus, was shot down on the eve of the 825th anniversary of Latvia’s capital of Riga. As the city celebrated, NATO organized a public event in front of a museum. Tanks were on display, and soldiers, flanked by NATO and Canadian flags, were talking with residents. Among them was Loreta Munda, a 17-year-old who plans to pursue a career in the military. “When I was younger, in 2014, I saw on the news what was happening in Ukraine. I thought to myself, ‘My God, if that happens here, I want to be among those who protect my country.’” With NATO forces present, Loreta says she feels safe. “I know there are soldiers ready to help us, but there are also plenty of people my age who are ready to defend our country.” In a country where the scars of Soviet history remain raw, Latvia is caught between Russian threats and the support of its NATO allies. This report was first published by The Canadian Press Aug. 22, 2026. Stéphane Blais, The Canadian Press

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: The extreme heat of the summer weather in France has caused grapes to wilt and be scalded. Photograph: sportpoint/Alamy View image in fullscreen The extreme heat of the summer weather in France has caused grapes to wilt and be scalded. Photograph: sportpoint/Alamy France French winemakers forecast 30-year low harvest after severe drought and heat Estimates suggest drop in production with vineyards also concerned ‘smoke taint’ from wildfires may affect quality Kim Willsher in Paris Mon 7 Sep 2026 11.10 EDT Last modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 11.19 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google French vineyards hit by severe drought and heatwaves are expected to report a 30-year low in wine production after the country’s hottest ever recorded summer, according to the agriculture ministry. Initial estimates suggest winemakers will produce just under 34m hectolitres from this year’s harvest: a drop of 6% on last year, and 17% less than ‌the 2021-2025 average. Agreste, the government’s farming food, forestry and fishing statistics body, said the drop was partly caused by a reduction in the number and size of vineyards, but mostly the result of extreme weather conditions . “The summer was particularly hot and dry: soil drought has intensified throughout the country and heatwaves have caused localised sun scald, scorching, defoliation, and wilting of the grapes, reducing harvest volumes,” it reported. View image in fullscreen A grape picker gets to work at the Trois Terres vineyard in Octon, southern France earlier this month. Photograph: Guillaume Horcajuelo/EPA However, some winemakers say with grape harvests still being conducted it is too early to make credible predictions. The disappointing forecast comes after an optimistic start to the year, with heavy spring rains that encouraged grape growth. “The hot and dry summer conditions meant a deterioration of the [harvest] forecast,” Agreste reported. A series of heatwaves brought the highest summer temperatures recorded in France since records began in 1900, with averages of 24C in June, July and August. Almost half of the country recorded temperatures on or above 40C. Among the worst hit wine regions is Champagne where the grape harvest, which started unusually early in mid August, is predicted to be almost half that of last year. The Jura region in the east was the next worst hit with an estimated 37% loss. This year’s Burgundy-Beaujolais region grape production was expected to be one-third down, Agreste reported. Winemakers in Bordeaux and the Languedoc-Roussillon as well as those in the south-east and south-west reported higher harvests this year but all except the Savoie region were down on the 2021-2025 five-year average for production. However, Cécile Mathiaud of the Burgundy wine producers association said she was surprised by the government’s disastrous figures for her region’s vineyards. “We know we won’t have a full harvest this year, but we have no definite figures and there’s no suggestion the situation is a disaster,” Mathiaud said. “We have some vineyards that have reported not much this year and others where it has been higher than expected.” View image in fullscreen The harvest under way early in the morning at Trois Terres. Photograph: Guillaume Horcajuelo/EPA Some Burgundy vineyards began their harvest in early August but others are collecting the grapes now, she added. “Our reference is the historically low harvest of 2021 when we produced only 1m hectolitres; we think it will be higher this year, but the question is by how much? I have absolutely no idea how the ministry has come up with these figures.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion Agreste said the figures were estimates and definitive results would not be known until regions made official harvest declarations later this year. It added that 2026 grape harvests were “marked by significant regional disparities”. Heatwaves and wildfires are setting back air quality improvements, UN finds Read more Wine harvests have traditionally taken place in France between September and mid October, but the climate emergency has brought dates forward slightly each year for the last four decades. This year, the harvest timetable advanced at least a week compared with last year throughout the country. Some vineyards in Bordeaux began two weeks early. There are also concerns that vines and grapes in some of France’s best-known wine producing regions, including Bordeaux, have been damaged by smoke from rampant wildfires. No major Bordeaux vineyards suffered direct damage from the flames that came within 15km (9 miles) of the city, but there is concern that smoke has entered the grape skins causing “smoke taint” and affecting the taste of the finished wine. The agriculture ministry would normally issue harvest estimates in early August, but postponed its analysis at the request of the wine industry because of what it described as “the high level of uncertainty surrounding these forecasts” caused by weather conditions and wildfires. France’s wine sector is already under pressure owing to a decline in demand. Annual wine consumption in the 1960s in France was 127 litres each year compared with 40 litres a year now. Wine drinking in the US, France’s largest export market, has also dropped and French wines have been hit by Donald Trump’s tariffs. https://www.politico.eu/article/andy-bur.text: LIVERPOOL, England — Andy Burnham is planning to go big on Brexit. For his party, the question is: How big? The U.K. prime minister is now widely expected to use his annual speech to Labour’s party conference in Liverpool on Tuesday to talk up closer ties with the EU. But Burnham will have to strike a delicate balance between those in his party who want to walk back Brexit — and those who want to make peace with it . Advertisement Advertisement Hours ahead of Burnham’s speech, cabinet members were far from speaking with one voice on the issue. Lucy Powell, Labour’s deputy leader, said at the POLITICO Pub on the sidelines of the conference that going beyond EU plans inherited from Keir Starmer for a reset of relations was “not possible nor desirable.” “I think there are ways we can improve our links on defense and security, but beyond that, I’m not going to speculate,” she added. Her comments came after Business and Trade Secretary Jonathan Reynolds on Sunday warned that “constitutional questions” around Britain's EU relationship were causing “uncertainty” for business. Also speaking at the POLITICO Pub, he warned against moves to join the customs union — which he said would involve the U.K. having to “accept a whole range of alignment on regulatory issues.” Yet Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told delegates from the main Labour conference stage that the U.K’s future lay in a “deeper” partnership with the EU. Advertisement Advertisement “Europe is not just our geography, but so much more,” he said. “It is how we pursue our values from climate to the Middle East. It's how we pursue our interests from trade to defense. It's where we build and protect our alliances … I say to this conference, our future lies in a stronger, deeper partnership with the European Union.” Mayor of London Sadiq Khan, meanwhile, said the U.K.’s return to the EU is inevitable and that Burnham should start preparing the British public for that reality. Further and faster Burnham’s recently appointed EU Relations Minister Hamish Falconer told Labour conference delegates on Monday that the prime minister wanted to go “further and faster” than his predecessor. Falconer, a former hostage negotiator who served in Britain’s diplomatic corps before being elected to parliament in 2024, confirmed the public would “hear a bit from the prime minister” on the EU. At a packed rally of Labour activists on Sunday, Stella Creasy, the MP who chairs the Labour Movement for Europe caucus urged Burnham to drop Keir Starmer’s “red lines” in negotiations with the bloc. Starmer's manifesto pledges rule out membership of the single market, customs union and free movement — and make a much closer deal with Brussels all-but impossible. Advertisement Advertisement “Who starts a negotiation with a list of what you don’t want — apart from a toddler?” Creasy told her audience to rapturous applause — urging the government to instead draw up a “list of common goals” with the EU: “Let us say it proudly and clearly: drop the red lines now.” Speaking at another event on Monday as news that Burnham was likely to address the issue filtered through conference, Creasy said that “what comes out tomorrow” should “set a plan of action” and amount to “more than warm words.” Question of strategy The divide is partly a disagreement over political strategy. Labour figures disagree on whether relitigating Brexit is a good use of their political time. Proponents of a closer relationship say the issue is well-placed to enthuse and win back defectors to the Greens and Liberal Democrats. Skeptics say it will do more to turn off voters wary of well-worn debates and prime proponents of Brexit to accuse politicians of betraying the will of the people. There are genuine economic disagreements, too. Whether the U.K. could prosper as a rule-taker inside the single market but outside the EU and whether its independent trade policy is worth sacrificing for a customs union are genuine matters of debate in the party. Question marks also hang over how straightforward rejoining the bloc wholesale would be and whether the U.K. could get its old deal back. Advertisement Advertisement Yet even if Burnham does stand up on Tuesday and promise a closer relationship with Europe, it could be easier said than done. Current talks on Starmer’s relatively modest “reset” over an agriculture and food trade deal, youth visas, and coordination on emissions have proved harder to seal than anticipated. A summit scheduled for July and postponed when Burnham took over is yet to get a new date, despite him having a sit-down meeting with the European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at the United Nations General Assembly last week. An ever-expanding set of issues The scope of talks has started to creep ever larger. London wants Brussels to give guarantees British businesses won’t be hit by new Made in Europe rules — while Brussels says it can’t be done. “In the short term I’m quite gloomy. I think the summit which was supposed to happen in November may not happen at all,” Charles Grant, director of the Centre for European Reform think-tank told a fringe event. “Unless someone is willing to compromise there may not be a summit at all this year, I hope I’m wrong on that.” Jukka Salovaara, the EU’s recently-appointed ambassador in London stuck a more optimistic tone. “My own expectation is for a summit to happen in November,” he said. “True that there are many issues that need to be solved but that’s why we are working on them and making sure that we take a step forward. Summits are never an end in itself, it’s always about what we achieve together and where we can go.” Advertisement Advertisement

Home Posts Signal #91: Meta is selling $97.5B of itself Signal #91: Meta is selling $97.5B of itself Meta is selling $97.5 billion of its own stock to pay for AI, Microsoft offered buyouts to a quarter of its staff, the whole of CEE raised €632 million in a quarter, and Europe's €30 billion gigafactory call got zero bids. Çelik Nimani Oct 27, 2026 • 4 min read In partnership with Morning, friends. For two years the question was who would build the best model. This week the question became who can afford to keep paying for one. The richest companies on earth are now selling shares and trimming payroll to buy chips, and that changes the maths for everyone downstream, including us. The CEE funding numbers are the ones to read slowly. The Microsoft piece has a hiring opportunity hidden in it. Four stories, five minutes. Meta can't pay for AI out of what it earns Meta launched the largest corporate share sale on record on 26 October and lifted it to $97.5 billion a day later: $25 billion of common stock at $625 a share, about $12.5 billion of preferred shares, and up to $60 billion more sold gradually once new non-voting shares start trading in early 2027. Nvidia is buying $3 billion of it . The reason sits in last week's results. Meta's free cash flow went negative for the first time in over a decade, minus $2.1 billion against plus $10.6 billion a year earlier, while it guided $135 to $145 billion of AI hardware spend. The best ad machine ever built now needs outside money to keep buying GPUs. Alphabet sold $84.75 billion of stock in June. And the company selling the chips is now buying the customer's shares to fund its own orders. Two things to watch. GPU demand looks stronger when suppliers finance their buyers, so treat "sold out" signals with some suspicion. And the cloud prices you pay are now backed by shareholder patience, not cash. Lock longer price terms on compute while they are still on offer. The AI notetaker that gets the hard words right Your AI is only as good as what you feed it. Feed it a transcript with your product names, acronyms, and numbers spelled wrong, and you spend the afternoon hand-fixing the output. Wispr Flow Notetaker uses your dictionary and calendar, so product names, acronyms, numbers, and uncommon names come out spelled right. It pops up when your meeting starts and captures Zoom, Google Meet, Teams, and Slack huddles with one click, no bot joining the call. Then your meetings show up inside Claude or ChatGPT through the built-in connector. No copy paste. Try Notetaker free on Mac and Windows. Try Notetaker Free All of CEE raised less than 1% of Meta's cheque Startups across Central and Eastern Europe raised €632 million in Q3 across 118 rounds, according to Vestbee's report out today. That is up 24% on a year ago, but the deal count dropped from 143, and the region still takes only 2.8% of European venture money. Meta's share sale alone is roughly 130 times the whole quarter. The money is bunched at the top. Bulgaria's EnduroSat (€186.4 million) and Lithuania's Oxylabs (€118.2 million) took 48% of it, which is why Bulgaria led the table with €200.6 million. About a third of notable rounds went to AI companies, yet 12 of the 17 that disclosed amounts raised under €2.5 million. The region is funding AI products on seed cheques while the infrastructure under them gets bought with tens of billions. That gap is the opening, not the excuse. Nobody here will outspend Meta on chips, but every company paying for those chips wants them used more cheaply: routing, evaluation, smaller models, smarter caching. Build what makes expensive compute go further, and plan your round on the real numbers. Poland's median seed round was about €1.1 million. Microsoft is paying for GPUs with payroll Microsoft offered voluntary buyouts to around 60,000 employees on 26 October, its first company-wide exit offer for staff at vice-president level and below. Xbox, Windows, Copilot and Finance teams in the US, Canada, India and the UK are included, about 27% of its 223,000 people. Data-centre and sales staff are left out . Read the exclusions. The people who build capacity and the people who sell it stay. Everyone else is now spending that competes with GPUs. Buyouts are the quiet version of a layoff: no headline count, and the most employable people leave first. An earlier retirement-age offer had 8,750 eligible and more than 30% said yes. Microsoft reports results tomorrow, with cloud growth guided near 45%. The interesting part for founders is what happens next. Thousands of experienced product, platform and finance people, many in India and the UK, may be on the market by the end of the year with a severance cushion. Set up a remote-friendly senior role now, before the big companies that are still hiring get there first. Brussels offered €10 billion and nobody bid The EU's call for AI gigafactories offers up to €10 billion of public money to pull in at least €20 billion of private capital, for up to seven sites. With weeks still to go before its 12 November deadline, it had received no proposals at all , so Brussels pushed the deadline to 3 December, as reported on 22 October. It is not a lack of interest. France and Czechia signed a compute pact on 23 October, with France's Bull joining the Czech bid led by České Radiokomunikace. The Dutch prime minister backed a 600 MW, 250,000-GPU campus in Rotterdam, then ruled out paying the public share the EU expects. Europe has the money and the land. What it lacks is someone willing to carry the risk Meta is covering by selling its own stock. Watch 3 December. If bids arrive, consortium seats open for grid, cooling, integration and software partners, and the Czech bid is the nearest one for companies in our region. If the call slips again, expect the terms to get better before the deadline does. Short Signals Dev: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B runs an agent on your laptop. NVIDIA's new open model has 4 billion effective parameters and fits in about 4GB of video memory, so a local voice or tool-calling agent no longer needs a cloud bill. Try it on one internal task that touches data you don't want leaving the building. ( MarkTechPost ) Productivity: GitHub Copilot now lives inside Microsoft Teams. Tag @GitHub on a bug report in a Teams thread and Copilot opens a pull request with a proposed fix. Install the new app this week: the legacy GitHub app for Teams retires on 16 November. ( GitHub changelog ) Design: Figma's MCP server can now call video and image models. Agents working through the Figma MCP can generate with Seedance, Kling and Nano Banana inside your file, paid with Weave credits. Wire it into your design agent and generate motion drafts next to the frames they belong to. ( Releasebot ) Marketing: From 30 October, Meta's AI edits to your ads are your responsibility. Meta's updated terms make advertisers solely responsible for changes its AI makes to their creative. Before Black Friday, open every Advantage+ campaign and switch off the creative toggles you haven't checked. ( PPC Land ) Dev: Replit's Monitoring Agent reads your production logs. It watches logs and metrics on live apps, proposes fixes and validates them, with auto-fix optional. Point it at one small production app and see what it catches in a week.
